summary: The note describes a fictional-seeming news story about a "solar tsunami" observed on October 11th, 2023, a solar flare combined with a coronal mass ejection that disrupted satellites, GPS, and power grids on Earth. It covers expert commentary, community responses, the creation of the International Space Weather Initiative, an AI early warning system, economic losses, and growing public and scientific focus on space weather preparedness.
one_line: A 2023 solar tsunami, a flare plus coronal mass ejection, disrupted Earth's satellites, GPS and power grids, spurring global preparedness and mitigation efforts.
key_facts: On October 11th, 2023, astronomers at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory in Hawaii observed a "solar tsunami" surging across the sun's surface toward Earth.
The solar tsunami was caused by a sudden release of magnetic energy in the form of a solar flare combined with a coronal mass ejection (CME).

Dr. Leila Vargas, a solar physicist, said solar tsunamis are not inherently destructive by cosmic standards because Earth's magnetosphere usually shields the planet, but a convergence of solar anomalies amplified this event.
Solar activity usually follows an 11-year cycle, and the 2023 solar season proved more tempestuous than anticipated.
Global satellite communications were significantly disrupted, and auroras reached lower latitudes as far south as the Caribbean.
Dr. Rajeev Singh of the Toulouse Space Center had predicted dire effects; GPS systems faltered, causing navigation confusion and the grounding of international flights as a precaution.
In Amsterdam, local Ham radio operators built an impromptu communication network connecting emergency services when digital systems failed.
Adriana Lima, a community leader in São Paulo, organized neighborhoods to share resources during blackouts caused by geomagnetic-induced currents in power lines.
Dr. Hiro Tanaka of the University of Tokyo said investing in resilient power grids, enhanced forecasting models, and hardened satellite systems is "a requirement for sociotechnical stability."

The newly-formed International Space Weather Initiative (ISWI) aims to unite political, scientific, and industry leaders and promoted technology to automatically reroute power and communications during space weather events.
Dr. Emily Patterson of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and her team developed an AI-based early warning system using deep learning to predict solar events more accurately.
Economist Dr. Khalil Rahman of the London School of Economics estimated billions in losses from disrupted commerce and repair costs.
Dr. Vargas led an international campaign for more robust solar observatories, saying "The more accurate data we can gather, the better we can prepare."
Universities expanded space weather departments to train specialists in heliophysics, and public seminars on solar tsunami preparedness became as common as those for hurricanes and earthquakes.
